en: Homage to the glorious Vajraḍāka!

In the language of India: *Śrī Hevajra-nāma-sādhanam*. In the language of Tibet: *Dpal kye rdo rje zhes bya ba'i sgrub pa'i thabs* (The Sadhana Entitled "Glorious Hevajra"). Homage to Hevajra! I bow to that Holder of the Vajra, who is seated within the syllable *Evaṃ*, who is the Lord born from the four joys, and who is free from beginning, middle, and end.
O Lord, you who abide as the very nature of *e* and *vaṃ*, the four protectors, liberated from beginning, end, and middle— to you, the Vajradhara, I prostrate.
Having paid homage with devotion to the Guru, the Buddhas, and the Saṅgha,
as well as to Caryāvajra and the other elders, I shall explain the *Hevajrasādhana*.
Having prostrated with devotion at the feet of the Guru, the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the elders, one should write.
The place for the time of initial practice should be chosen as auspicious;
staying there, the mantra practitioner achieves success through single-minded concentration.
First, the teaching on the place of practice is as follows: "Meditation is said to be auspicious in a solitary tree, or in a cemetery,
or likewise in a mother's house at night, or in a secluded wilderness."
It is taught that meditation is excellent in a solitary tree, in a charnel ground, likewise in the houses of *mātṛkā*s, or else in a secluded place or a remote hermitage.
One should visualize the syllable *raṃ* in one's own heart; from it arises a sun-maṇḍala, and right there, one should visualize the syllable *hūṃ*, which is the very nature of wisdom and method.

Since it is stated thus, one should sit in that place or in a location where one feels joy, and having practiced the yoga of equanimity in single-pointed meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one should dwell at night within one's own heart. From *RAṂ* arises a sun mandala; upon that is the syllable *HŪṂ*, the essence of method and wisdom.
Having beheld the Lord, the Master, the Lord of Vajras, in the sky—
One should worship with the eight goddesses, who wear all manner of ornaments.
Having seen the Guru, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas in the sky, he emanated eight goddesses adorned with ornaments and made offerings:
Gaurī holds a deer-marked [moon] disc; Caurī holds a vessel of the sun;
Vetālī holds water in her hand; and Ghasmarī holds medicine.
Gaurī holds a vessel of moonlight; Caurī holds a vessel of sunlight; Vetālī holds a vessel of scented water; Ghasmarī holds a vessel of medicine.
Pukkasī has a vajra in her hand, and Śavarī likewise holds a vessel of flavors.
Caṇḍālī plays the hand-drum (ḍamaruka); with these [goddesses], one should worship the Lord.
Pukkasī, the Vajra-holder; Śavarī, the vessel of nectar; Caṇḍālī, the holder of the small drum—may they offer worship.
Having thus worshipped [the one] whose neck is embraced by Ḍombī out of passion for great desire, one should perform the confession and so forth with the outer offerings.
One should practice great passion and subsequent attachment inseparable from the tactile sensation of the consort (*dombinī*). Then, perform the outer offerings, the confession of misdeeds, and:

*ratnatrayaṃ me śaraṇaṃ sarvaṃ pratidiśāmy aham |* *anumode jagatpuṇyaṃ buddhabodhau dadhe manaḥ ||* The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all [misdeeds]. I rejoice in the merit of the world and fix my mind upon the awakening of a Buddha.
One should take refuge in the Three Jewels and so forth.
First, one should cultivate loving-kindness; thereafter, one should meditate on compassion. Third, one should cultivate sympathetic joy, and finally, equanimity toward all remaining beings.
Then, first one should cultivate loving-kindness, second compassion, third joy, and fourth equanimity.
One should then make the mind empty in order to abandon ordinary ego-grasping;
thereafter, one makes the mind emptiness, so that cyclic existence may be rendered devoid of grasping at a self.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham / Having visualized a sun disk in front by means of the syllable *repha*, one should visualize a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) arising from a *hūṃ* below it;
and by that very vajra, one should visualize a rampart and the binding of a cage.

Then, one should meditate on a sun mandala arising from the syllable RAṂ. Upon that, from the syllable HŪṂ, there arises a vajra; at its hub is the syllable HŪṂ. From it, rays of light radiate forth, whereby a canopy, the ground, and walls are formed.
"Having meditated on the bhaga within the *khadhātu*, one should perform the meditation in the center:
first the wheel, then the earth, the water, and according to the proper order, the fire."
For the deities, there is the Great Wind and the emanator according to their arising;
and the wheel born from the source of phenomena (dharmodaya), adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces.
It is four-cornered with four gates, adorned with vajra-lines;
it is joined with vajra-lines and beautified by a profusion of various flowers.
In the center of that, one should meditate on the source of the expanse of space as the mandalas of wind, fire, water, and earth.

Above that, from *bhrūṃ*, arises a wheel with *bhrūṃ* at its hub; from the inseparability of these two—the *bhrūṃ* and the wheel—Vairocana emerges. He merges into one with the maṇḍala of the four elements, and in the center of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), it becomes a celestial palace (*vimāna*). This single-storied palace has four doors, adorned with four archways, and possesses the form of various flowers.
The seed-syllables of the moon, the vowels, and the sun should be situated in the center.
One should visualize the reality-syllable HŪṂ situated in the center of the vajra-navel.
Furthermore, the mirror-like wisdom is the moon; the wisdom of equality is the one with seven times seven [minds];
and the wisdom of discernment is said to be the seed-syllables and the marks of the deity.
The wise practitioner should effect the unification with all [deities] through the purity of the manifestation of the image, cultivating the form by means of the five methods that have been taught.
One should visualize the Lord of the Maṇḍala, arisen from the reflection of the sentient being,
possessing the Vajra insignia and other marks like a son, with the luster of a moonstone gem.
Eight-faced and four-legged, adorned with sixteen arms,
he is joined in sexual union with Nairātmyā, locked in an embrace.
In the past, in a delightful city, you and I were absorbed in the pleasures of play;
Gaurī emerged at the eastern gate from the union of the churner and the churning-stick, and Caurikā emerged once more.
Having emerged at the southern gate, Caurī is the excellent gatekeeper;
then, through the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*, Vetālī emerges once more.
Emerging from the western gate, Morabhañjanī is seated;
furthermore, Ghasmarī has emerged during the great union of the couple.
Having emerged, she sat at the northern gate, possessing a terrible form;
furthermore, from the friction and union of the two, Pukkasī emerged.
Having emerged, she sits in the northeast corner, possessing a terrible form;
again, by means of the churning yoga, Śavarī is in the southeast corner.

Caṇḍālī is in the direction of the Rākṣasas (the southwest), and Ḍombī is in the corner of Māruta (the northwest). In their center, from *ali* arises a moon mandala; from *kāli* arises a sun mandala. The moon is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), and the sun is the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). In their center, from *hūṃ*, arises a vajra, which is the wisdom of individual discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Its essence, in which [the two] are merged as one, is the wisdom of all-accomplishing action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). It takes the form of Vajrasattva, which is the wisdom of the utterly pure sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātupariśuddhajñāna*).

From the mixed syllable *hūṃ*, Vajrasattva is generated through the five stages of manifest enlightenment (*pañcābhisambodhi*). His faces and hand-symbols correspond to those of the Father and Son [the central deities]. He has the form of Vajrasattva-Ratnacandra, with sixteen arms, eight faces, and four legs, bringing joy. With his first two hands, he embraces Nairātmyā.

The moon of the non-dual bodhicitta of method and wisdom abides in Gaurī in the direction of Indra; Tsaurī abides in the direction of the pretas; Vetālī abides in the direction of Varuṇa; and Ghasmarī abides in the direction of the yakṣas, in the manner of subduing the four māras. They abide at the gates in the form of those who strike down [the obstacles]. Pukkasi, having the form of one who strikes down, abides in the direction of Īśāna.
Śabarī resides in the southeast; Caṇḍālī resides in the southwest; and Ḍombinī resides in the northwest.
One should emanate these [goddesses] from the seed-syllables *gaṃ*, *caṃ*, *vaṃ*, *ghaṃ*, *puṃ*, *śaṃ*, *saṃ*, *caṃ*, and *ṭaṃ*.
Having completed their bodies from the seed-syllables *gaṃ*, *tsaṃ*, *baṃ*, *ghaṃ*, *baṃ*, *saṃ*, *laṃ*, and *ḍaṃ*, they should be brought forth.

Gaurī holds a curved knife in her right hand and a fish in her left; Tsaurī holds a small stone in her right and a pig in her left; Ghasmarī holds a snake in her right and a lotus vessel in her left; Pukkasi holds a lion in her right and an executioner’s sword in her left; Śabarī holds a monk in her right and a pebble in her left; Caṇḍālī holds a wheel in her right and a skull-cup in her left; Ḍombinī holds a vajra in her right and makes the threatening gesture with her left. Gaurī is black in color.

Caurī is red in color; Vetālī is yellow; Ghasmarī is green; Pukkasī is blue; Śabarī is white; Caṇḍālī has the color of the sky; and Ḍombinī has all various colors. All have three eyes, loose hair, and possess the four mudrās. They all stand with one leg extended and the other drawn in, each having two arms. [And] Brahmā...

Viṣṇu, Rudra, Yama, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Asuras, as well as Gaurī and the others, are their seats. Then, Vajrasattva together with his consort melts through great passion; thereupon, exhorted by the four goddesses and worshipped with various songs, he says: "O Hevajra, whose mind is compassion, Pukkasī, protect me!"

Desiring to engage in great bliss, arise by clearing away the nature of emptiness! Having cleared away the nature of emptiness, grant the *siddhi* upon the earth! If you wish to remain alive, please arise, Hevajra! Since I, Caṇḍālī, have not seen you, why do you remain in emptiness? Act as a hero according to your former vow!

"I am marked with the sign of Dombī; your mind is wisdom. It is not right for you to be without compassion; please arise like a magical illusion! First is the empty bodhicitta; in the second, the seed-syllable arises; in the third, the form is perfected; in the fourth, the letters are inscribed. The two seeds of the Lord and the Joyful One, and the two blue Fearless Ones in between."

From the light rays of the two syllables *aṃ* and *hūṃ*, the Great Vajra arises. Emanating in the form of a deity, it completely fills the expanse of space. Having withdrawn [the emanations] back into the *aṃ* and *hūṃ* at the heart, the yogin becomes the very nature of great hatred, known as *vajradhara*. With his four feet treading upon the earth, he strikes terror into the gods and asuras; black in color, he inspires fear.

Bestowing bliss upon Nairātmyā, she attains non-conceptual bliss. Her form is non-conceptual by nature; with her feet, she successively tramples the four Māras. She strikes terror into all fears; she completes the garland of severed heads. She performs a dance upon a sun-disc seat; a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) rests upon her crown. Black in color and terrifying, her first face is a great black one.

The face on the right is white like the moon; the face on the left is red and terrifying; the blue face above is wrathful. He possesses twenty-four eyes, and his other faces are black. He utters the sound "HŪṂ" and claps his hands.

The body is likewise smeared [with ashes]. Her eyebrows and hair are disheveled and yellow; her body is adorned with the five mudrās. Her eyes gaze with a wrathful stare. She is about sixteen years of age. An elephant, a horse, a donkey, an ox, a female camel, humans, a cat, and a lion—

In his right hands are eight skull-cups (kapāla), which are placed in succession as follows: the deity of Earth, the deity of Water, the deity of Fire, the deity of Wind, the deity of the Moon, the deity of the Sun, the deity of Yama, and Vaiśravaṇa. In his left hands are eight *bandhas*, which are likewise arranged in order: the Graceful, the Heroic, the Terrifying, the Laughing, the Wrathful, the Frightening, and [the remaining two].

Compassion, the fierce, the peaceful, and so forth, endowed with the nine dramatic sentiments (*navarasa*). *Śrī* is non-dual primordial wisdom; *He* is the complete abandonment of causes and so forth; *Ru* is being free from the aggregates (*skandha*); *Ka* is not abiding anywhere. *Oṃ dharmadhātu svabhāva ātmako ’haṃ*. For the two eyes is Mohavajra (Vajra of Delusion); for the ears is Dveṣavajra (Vajra of Hatred); for the nose is Mātsaryavajra (Vajra of Avarice).

In the mouth is Rāgavajrī; in the tangible is Īrṣyāvajrī; in the mind is Nairātmyayoginī; on the earth is Khecarī, the All-Vajrī; in the sky is Ghoṣavajrī. Abiding in the center of the heart is Nairātmyā. From the seed-syllable at one's own heart, black light resembling a hook radiates forth, inviting the Buddhas of the three realms.

The offering should be performed by the eight goddesses. Then, one should make this supplication: OṂ ABHIṢIÑCATU MĀṂ SARVA-VAJRA-TATHĀGATA. Having completed [the recitation], all are Heruka. May the empowerment be conferred by all the Buddhas; may the empowerment be conferred with the vase of nectar, which is the nature of all the Buddhas. Then, there is a rain of flowers, cloth, and sandalwood powder.

As the rain of *gur-gum* falls, the expanse of space is filled with various sounds; having performed worship through various forms, the translators and others also offer praise with vajra songs. Having thus completed the empowerment, Akṣobhya in the form of a wheel and Amitābha in the form of an ear...

One should recollect oneself as having Ratnasambhava at the neck, Amoghasiddhi as the belt, and Vairocana as the nature of the bracelets. The five mudrās are the purification of the five families. Red eyes are the purification of compassion; a black complexion is the purification of loving-kindness.

The purity of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) is the skin; the purity of the four noble truths (āryasatya) is the bone; the purity of the mudrās is the five Buddhas. He has the form of a wrathful deity (*krodha*) for the sake of subduing malevolent sentient beings. The purity of flesh is Pukkasī; the purity of blood is Śabarī; the purity of awakening is Caṇḍālī; and the purity of marrow is Ḍombinī.

The eight faces are the complete purity of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). The three eyes are the complete purity of the body, speech, and mind. The sixteen hands are the complete purity of the sixteen emptinesses (*śūnyatā*). The four legs are the complete purity of the four Māras. The four mudrās are the Tathāgatas Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Gaurī, and so forth.

The purification of earth is Pukkasi; the purification of water is Bāri; the purification of fire is Caṇḍālī; and the purification of wind is stated to be Ḍombinī. Having arisen from abiding in the three times, one should assume the form of the deity. If free from afflictions, one should perform the mantra recitation: OṂ DEVA PIṢU VAJRA HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. All activities should be performed in the form of Heruka.

Whatever siddhi one desires, one should assume the form of Heruka. If one remains for six months, the siddhi will arise; provided there is no deluded thought, one will attain the miraculous powers of a Buddha. All movement and gesture are mudrās, and all speech is mantra. This is the abiding state of Heruka.

Consciousness is authentic knowledge; this is the summary of the *sādhana* from the *Tantra*. Since it does not depend on knowing or not knowing, it clarifies the profound method. From the ocean of the milk of wisdom, the momentary oral instructions were extracted with the wood-spoon of the master’s pith instructions. Just as one who eats nectar [is satisfied], so too was the mind of that [disciple] [filled].

This *Heruka-sādhana*, which has been clearly elucidated, is based upon the *Hevajra-tantra*. Through this merit of mine, and through the merit arising from reciting the glorious sequence of mantras according to the stages taught therein, may all sentient beings be swiftly liberated by means of the sublime virtue of awakening. May my teachers, parents, and retinue hear this with joy.

Through this composition concerning the *bodhimaṇḍa*, by means of the primordial wisdom of recollection (*pūrvānusmṛti-jñāna*), may the glorious one attain the realization of suchness. This concludes the *Hevajra-sādhana* composed by the master Bodhigarbha. It was translated and finalized by the Indian preceptor Dampa Karacandra and the Tibetan translator Lha bTsan-po Mu-ni-rāja.

Having composed this very clear *Heruka-sādhana*, which accords with the sequence of the language [of the original] as set forth in the *Hevajra-tantra*, I have acquired this much merit. By this, may all sentient beings—whose minds are obscured by the spreading poison of the faults of wrong views and whose inclinations are toward worldly pleasure—become single-mindedly intent upon happiness, possessing the nature of the glorious womb of awakening (*bodhigarbha*). Thus ends the *Śrīheruka-sādhana* spoken in the Noble Language (*Āryabhāṣā*).
This is the work of the venerable teacher Garbhapāda (or Bodhigarbhapāda).
